sections.text:
The letter opens with someone who cannot stop talking about what he has seen and heard. It is about the Word of life, which they heard, saw and handled, until “our hands touched” it. The writer says it plainly: they declare it so that their readers may share in it.

He writes to reassure a community shaken by people who have left it. His letter keeps circling three marks of real faith: believing that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh, obeying God’s commands, and loving one another.

Two statements hold the letter together. The first is “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.” The second is “God is love.” Love is known by this, he says: that God sent his Son.

He says why he is writing in the closing chapter: he wants those who believe to know they have eternal life.

The letter names no author. Tradition links it, and the two short letters that follow, with the apostle John and the church in Ephesus near the end of the first century. Its language is very close to that of John’s Gospel.

The letter says both that anyone who claims to be without sin is deceived and that those born of God do not go on sinning. Readers generally understand the second as describing a settled way of life, not single failures. Some older English Bibles include a longer sentence about three heavenly witnesses at 5:7 that is absent from the early Greek copies and from most Bibles today.
